title: How to Preach Doctrine Without Losing the Room
subtitle: A practical guide to preaching doctrine and theology in sermons so that truth like justification, the Trinity, and the atonement lands on real lives instead of going over heads.

sections.title: Why Preachers Dodge Doctrine
sections.body:
We say we want our people to know God. Then we preach a steady diet of tips and avoid the doctrine that would actually reveal him.

The fear is real and almost noble. We have sat under the dry theologian who emptied the room while he diagrammed the Trinity, and we swore we would never be him. So we go the other way. We preach the practical, the relatable, the takeaway you can use by Tuesday, and we tell ourselves we are meeting people where they are. We are. We are also leaving them there. A church fed only on application becomes a church that knows what to do and has no idea who God is. The doing has no root. The first hard wind tears it out.

The problem was never doctrine. The problem was doctrine preached as if it had nothing to do with anyone's life. That is not depth. That is a failure to finish the work.

sections.title: Every Doctrine Was Born in a Crisis
sections.body:
The great doctrines are not abstractions the church invented to have something to argue about. They were hammered out in fires, by people who needed them to survive.

The church did not define the two natures of Christ as an intellectual exercise. It defined them because if Jesus is not fully God he cannot save you, and if he is not fully man he did not save you, and people's hope hung on the difference. Justification by faith was not a theory. It was a drowning man finding the rock. The Trinity is not a math problem. It is the astonishing news that God was love before there was anyone to love, that relationship is the deepest thing in the universe. Find the crisis the doctrine answers, and you have found your sermon.

When you preach a doctrine, ask first what it costs to not believe it. Who falls apart without this. What lie does it kill. Doctrine preached as the answer to a real human ache is never boring. It is rescue.

sections.title: Make the Invisible Visible
sections.body:
Abstraction is the enemy. Not because your people are simple, but because no one lives in the abstract.

Do not say God is immutable. Say God will not be different tomorrow than he was the day he made his promise to you, and let your people feel the floor that puts under their feet. Do not say we are justified. Say the verdict that should fall at the end of your life has already been spoken over you, not guilty, and it will not be revised. The doctrine of the incarnation lands when you make your people see the maker of galaxies nursing at a teenage girl's breast. The same truth, dressed in flesh, walks into the room. The bare proposition stayed at the door.

This is what Jesus did with the kingdom of God, the deepest doctrine he taught, and he taught it with a mustard seed, a lost coin, a man beaten on a road. Concreteness is not dumbing down. It is the discipline of making truth visible enough to be believed.

sections.title: One Doctrine, Not Five
sections.body:
The sermon that tries to teach everything teaches nothing. Pick one truth and drive it home.

The temptation with doctrine is to pour out everything you learned in the study. You spent the week deep in the atonement and now you want to give them penal substitution and Christus Victor and the moral influence theory and the ransom and the recapitulation, all in thirty minutes. They will drown. Choose the single facet this text actually presents, and spend your whole sermon making that one thing unforgettable. Depth is not the number of ideas you cover. Depth is how far down you take one of them.

The theologian wants to be comprehensive. The preacher wants to be remembered. After your sermon a member should be able to carry one true thing about God out the door and hold it for a week. Not a survey. One stone, set deep enough that it stays.

sections.title: Doctrine That Ends in Worship
sections.body:
You have not finished preaching a doctrine until your people want to fall down.

Paul does this every time. He climbs through three chapters of the densest theology in Romans, election and grace and the fate of Israel, and at the top of the argument he does not give an application. He breaks into praise. O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God. That is the test of doctrinal preaching. Did it produce more information, or did it produce wonder. If your people leave knowing more about God but loving him no more than when they walked in, the doctrine sat in the head and never reached the heart.

This is the whole point. Sound doctrine is not the destination. It is the road, and the destination is a God so glorious that knowing him truly makes you worship. Preach so that the truth about God ends in the worship of God. Anything less is just a lecture with a Bible on the lectern.
